still_small.name: Pond, small lake
still_small.notes: A small volume of water warms and cools fastest. At night plants breathe instead of giving off oxygen, so it is lowest just before dawn: in an overgrown pond the water is oversaturated by evening and drops below two milligrams per litre before sunrise.

still_large.name: Large lake, reservoir
still_large.notes: Inert: it barely changes over a day, but the wind has room to build waves and mixing is serious.

flowing_small.name: Small river, stream
flowing_small.notes: The current aerates the water by itself and feeds it from above: daily swings are smoothed out and oxygen is enough even in the heat.

flowing_large.name: River
flowing_large.notes: The steadiest water body: temperature and oxygen change slowly, but the bottom relief and the current seams decide everything.

sea.name: Sea
sea.notes: The coefficients are tuned for the coastal strip within casting range from the shore: open water warms and cools more slowly than a river, the surf aerates it almost to the limit, and there is no stratification at this depth — it lies further out, beyond a shore cast. Tide, salinity and currents are not modelled: for the Baltic without pronounced tides that is not critical, but for seas with a strong tide or surge the shallows estimate will be rougher.

ocean.name: Ocean
ocean.notes: The value is declared but its behaviour is not described.

snags.name: Snags, sunken trunks
snags.notes: Works like an artificial reef: crayfish, larvae and fry live in the snags and a predator follows them.
snags.gear_note: Never let a fish run into the snag: the drag is locked and rods sit on stands. 0.40–0.45 mm mono, 0.60–0.70 mm shock leader and a forged thick-wire hook are about abrasion, not the weight of the fish.

bridge_piles.name: Jetty piles
bridge_piles.notes: The same snag, only man-made: shade, fouling and constant food.

undercut_bank.name: Undercut bank
undercut_bank.notes: Overhanging turf and exposed roots give shade, coolness and a constant fall of insects into the water.

point.name: Point, headland
point.notes: Feeding currents meet from both sides, and a predator patrols both flanks at once.

bay.name: Backwater, bay
bay.notes: Calm water with plankton and turbidity: the dining room of bream, crucian and roach.

steep_bank.name: Steep bank
steep_bank.notes: A sign that the drop-off and depth start right from the shore.

drop_off.name: Drop-off, edge
drop_off.notes: The boundary between depths: the path fish take to come out and feed and to leave and wait it out.

gravel_silt_edge.name: Gravel and silt edge
gravel_silt_edge.notes: The transition from hard bottom to soft: bloodworm live in the silt and are easy to take from the gravel. Carp follow such an edge like a drop-off.
gravel_silt_edge.gear_note: In deep silt the rig sinks: a 30–40 cm hooklink and a neutrally buoyant bait (pop-up or wafter) keep it visible.

flooded_channel.name: Flooded channel
flooded_channel.notes: An old river bed under a reservoir is a ready-made road: fish travel along it, not across. Depths of 4–12 m, with flooded forest and snags nearby.

shell_bed.name: Shell bed
shell_bed.notes: A zebra mussel colony is a permanent table and hard bottom: food lies in the open instead of sinking into silt.

hump.name: Hump, underwater rise
hump.notes: A local rise of the bottom: a predator stands on it above its prey and strikes from above.

inflow.name: Inflow, feeding stream
inflow.notes: Brings food and oxygen and washes up a cone of bottom sediment.

outflow.name: Outflow, draining channel
outflow.notes: The current draws fry out of the lake, and pike and zander wait in this funnel.

spring.name: Bottom spring
spring.notes: A local thermoregulator: in heat and in frost fish gather around the spring outlet.

reeds.name: Reeds, weed edge
reeds.notes: Shelter and food base at once: fry have somewhere to hide and peaceful fish have something to eat.

foam_line.name: Foam and duckweed in the downwind corner
foam_line.notes: The wind drives plankton and insects here, and the duckweed film gives shade.

windward_shore.name: Windward shore, surf
windward_shore.notes: Waves wash larvae out of the shore and bottom and saturate the water with oxygen. A wind in the face is awkward for the angler and good for the fish.

slack_water.name: Slack water, eddy behind an island
slack_water.notes: In a current fish stand where they do not have to row: behind an island, in an eddy, at the edge of a snag pile. Food is carried past and no energy is spent.
slack_water.gear_note: Hold the spot in the flow: a flat lead of 150–200 g, a rear weight presses the line to the bottom — otherwise the rig drifts and collects debris.

rotten_silt.name: Rotten silt, rainbow film
rotten_silt.notes: Gas bubbles and oily streaks betray decay: there is no oxygen here and the fish leave.

water.name: Plain water
water.notes: An ordinary stretch of water: outlined, but nothing stands out.

shore.name: Shore, access
shore.notes: A place where you can stand and approach the water.

beach.name: Beach, sandy shore
beach.notes: A sandy bottom feeds burrowing worms and small crustaceans — a table for flounder and cod patrolling the surf line.

rocky_shore.name: Rocky shore, boulders
rocky_shore.notes: Stones and weed hold crabs and small fish: a predator works the ridge like a snag pile in fresh water.

jetty_pier.name: Jetty, pier
jetty_pier.notes: Piles and the jetty wall are fouled with mussels and weed, give shade and break the current — fish hold right at the wall.

river_mouth.name: River mouth
river_mouth.notes: Fresh runoff carries food out to sea; migratory fish — sea trout, salmon — hold at the boundary of fresh and salt water before entering the river.

lagoon.name: Lagoon, shallow bay
lagoon.notes: Warmed shallows behind a spit without waves: a feeding ground for juveniles and flounder.

bait_fish_panic.name: Splashes and panicking fry
bait_fish_panic.notes: Rings and chaotic jumps of fry: a direct sign of perch, pike or asp striking.

birds_diving.name: Birds diving over the water
birds_diving.notes: Gulls and terns dive where a predator has pushed fry up to the surface.

fish_rolling.name: Fish rolling on the surface
fish_rolling.notes: Peaceful fish come to the surface: they are here and they are feeding.

foam_ryaska.name: Foam and duckweed blown in
foam_ryaska.notes: The wind has gathered plankton and insects in a corner, and there is shade under the film.

rainbow_film.name: Rainbow film, gas bubbles
rainbow_film.notes: Rotting silt: there is no oxygen and the fish have left.

wind_turned.name: Wind has turned
wind_turned.notes: A front has passed over the water: food has been carried to the other shore and the fish must find a table again. The bite returns when the new wind settles.

north_wind.name: North wind picked up
north_wind.notes: Cold air chills the top layer. In cold water that is against the angler; in overheated water, on the contrary, it knocks down the heat and adds oxygen.

calm_heat.name: Calm in the heat, second day
calm_heat.notes: There is nothing to mix the column, and the water has stratified: warm top, cold bottom, a thermocline between them. Fish leave the top layer but do not go to the pit either — there is nothing to breathe there.

warm_spell.name: Warmer after the cold
warm_spell.notes: A few warm days lift cold water by a couple of degrees and the fish come out to feed. In spring such a trend matters more than the temperature itself.

muddy_water.name: Water muddied after rain
muddy_water.notes: Rain wash knocks fish off their usual places; peaceful fish tolerate turbidity better than predators.

feeder_flat.name: Feeder, flat method
feeder_flat.notes: The bait lies on the feeder at the bottom. It works when fish feed from the bottom and is useless when they are in mid-water.
feeder_flat.rig: A short hooklink of 8–12 cm: the bait lies right against the feed, otherwise the fish take the feeder rather than the hook.

carp_bottom.name: Carp bottom rig
carp_bottom.notes: A hair rig on the bottom with spot baiting. It needs an understanding of the bottom: without probing it is a lottery.
carp_bottom.rig: Simpler is more reliable: coated hooklink stripped 1.5–2 cm at the hook, Wide Gape or Curved Shank hook, hair 1–1.5 cm from the bend. It is not the hand that sets the hook but a 100–140 g lead; a safety clip drops it on a break-off and the fish leaves without a weight on the line.

float.name: Float tackle
float.notes: The only bottom tackle where the depth is easy to change: the setting changes in a minute.

zig_rig.name: Zig rig, fishing in mid-water
zig_rig.notes: The bait hangs half-way down. It is how you take carp that cruise above the bottom and ignore the feeder.
zig_rig.rig: A long hooklink from the lead to a floating bait: the depth is measured from the bottom, not from the surface.

surface.name: Surface fishing
surface.notes: Crust, floating pellets, dog biscuits. A summer evening and warm water are its time.
surface.rig: A controller or clear float 40–60 cm from the bait: it gives the cast and does not scare fish near the surface.

spinning.name: Spinning, artificial lure
spinning.notes: A search for active fish: you cover the water, not a spot.

jig.name: Jigging on the bottom
jig.notes: A stepped retrieve along drop-offs and snags when the predator stands low.

livebait.name: Livebait
livebait.notes: Works on passive fish when they ignore an artificial lure.

bottom_bait_sea.name: Bottom rod from the shore
bottom_bait_sea.notes: Static tackle with a bait on the bottom: flounder and cod take from the beach bottom or at a jetty without chasing a lure.
bottom_bait_sea.rig: A beachcaster or sliding rig with a pear lead of 80 g or more to hold against the surf; hooklink 30–50 cm.

float_sea_top.name: Float for a top predator
float_sea_top.notes: Garfish take right at the surface while chasing fry: the tackle holds the bait in the top layer, not on the bottom.
float_sea_top.rig: A sliding float set to the top layer, a strip of fish or a fry on the rig.

spot.name: Spot baiting
spot.notes: A dozen boilies and a PVA bag right at the bait. In cold water and on a pressured water a big spread alarms rather than gathers: the fish eat little and inspect every spot.

carpet.name: Carpet of small particles
carpet.notes: Hemp, small pellets, crushed boilies. Small and medium carp move in shoals and feed in competition — the carpet stokes that competition and bites come one after another.

line.name: Baiting line
line.notes: A strip of boilies 100–200 m long from a boat or a bait rocket across the fish's route. On big water a spot means nothing: the line intercepts the shoal where it travels.

program.name: Long programme, ALT
program.notes: Feed a sector for several days in a row and do not fish. The herd stops linking boilies with danger and includes the spot in its daily route — then big fish sit on it rather than youngsters.

soft_jig.name: Soft bait on a jig head
soft_jig.notes: An all-rounder for cold and deep water: you set the speed of presentation.

spinner.name: Spinner
spinner.notes: A strong signal in turbid water and on the shallows; often excessive for passive fish.

spoon.name: Spoon
spoon.notes: Slow play on the pauses is what cold water needs.

crank.name: Crankbait
crank.notes: Holds the depth: handy when you know at what depth the fish stand.

popper.name: Surface lure
popper.notes: Warm water and low light: a strike at the surface can be heard and seen.

jerk.name: Jerkbait, large minnow
jerk.notes: A large lure screens out small fish and takes trophy fish.

clear_bright.notes: In clear water in bright light the fish see the whole lure — naturalness and speed save the day.

clear_low.notes: At dawn and dusk a predator strikes the silhouette from below — dark reads better than bright.

stained_any.notes: In turbid water the lure is found by the lateral line, not the eyes: it needs sound and a noticeable colour.

dark_night.notes: At night the silhouette against the sky and vibration work, not the colouring.

cold_water.notes: In cold water a predator does not chase: the lure must be retrieved slowly and left to hang.
